vignette:
She is twenty-five years old, a counselor at a community mental health clinic in a midsized city. She came to therapy reluctantly, referred by her supervisor after three clients complained that she seemed distracted, even tearful during sessions. She hates that she is here. She is South Asian, single, lives alone in a small apartment near the clinic. She always thought of herself as someone who helped others hold their pain-now she cannot hold her own.

The event happened eleven months ago, on a cool October evening. She had stayed late to finish notes after a difficult session with a teenage client who had been in foster care. It was almost eight o'clock when she walked to her car in the clinic parking lot. She saw a police cruiser pull into the lot, and she did not think much of it-the clinic was near a busy street, and officers sometimes stopped for coffee at the corner shop. But this cruiser stopped directly behind her car, and two officers got out quickly. She remembers the sound of their boots on the asphalt, the glare of the headlights. One officer shouted something she could not process. She froze. The next seconds are fragmented: she was on the ground, her cheek pressed against cold gravel, an officer's knee in her back, her wrists yanked behind her. She screamed that she worked at the clinic, that she was a counselor, that she had done nothing wrong. The officers released her after ten minutes-a misidentification, they said. A suspect had been reported in the area, and she matched the description. No apology. Just a curt "You can go."

She drove home shaking, her hands numb on the steering wheel, her body vibrating. She did not sleep that night. She replayed it over and over: the knee, the shouting, the helplessness. For weeks afterward she felt a constant low hum of fear, a sense that safety was an illusion she had been naive to believe in. She started checking her rearview mirror obsessively when driving, especially if she saw a police car. She began taking a longer route to work to avoid the block where the clinic parking lot is, even though the lot itself is behind the building. She tells herself she is being practical, but she knows it is not practical-it is a ritual that drains her, and she does it anyway.

Her work has become a minefield. She is a good counselor-she was praised for her empathy and calm presence. Now she feels a knot in her stomach every time a client mentions an encounter with law enforcement. She finds herself steering the conversation away, asking questions that subtly change the subject. She knows she is failing her clients, but the alternative-hearing details of handcuffs, batons, shouted commands-makes her heart pound so hard she cannot think. Last month a client described being stopped for a broken tail light, and she had to excuse herself to the bathroom, where she stood gripping the sink, breathing in shallow gasps, her mind flashing to gravel and headlights.

She has nightmares two or three times a week. In the dreams she is back on the ground, but this time no one lets her go-they drag her away, she disappears into a system she cannot see. She wakes drenched in sweat, her sheets twisted, her throat raw from screaming that makes no sound. She avoids the news. She deletes social media apps from her phone because videos of police violence trigger waves of nausea and a sense of imminent doom. Her appetite is erratic; she has lost eight pounds without trying. She has stopped going to the gym because the gym is near a police station. She tells friends she is just busy.

She knows she is supposed to be the one who holds steady. She is a counselor. She has a master's degree in clinical mental health, a certification in trauma-informed care. She knows the textbook definitions of hyperarousal, avoidance, negative cognitions. But knowing does not stop her hands from trembling when an unmarked white van slows down near her on the street. It does not stop her from scanning every parking lot before she gets out of her car. It does not stop the shame that sits inside her like a stone: shame that she was a good South Asian daughter, a helper, a professional, and still the system threw her to the ground. Shame that she cannot get over it.

She is here now, in this therapist's office, because she had no other choice. She sits on the edge of the chair, her purse clutched in her lap, her eyes avoiding the clock. She says she does not know if talking will help. She says she is tired of being afraid. She says she wants to be the counselor she used to be. But her voice is thin, and she is already checking the parking lot through the window, even though the session has just begun.
